fetched_contents.text: Preventable risk factors for coronary heart disease and stroke amongst ethnic groups in London Ethn Health. 2001 May;6(2):87-94. doi: 10.1080/13557850120068414. Authors Affiliation * 1 Department of Public Health Sciences, King's College London, UK. * PMID: 11480964 * DOI: 10.1080/13557850120068414 Abstract Objectives: People of African Caribbean descent have higher mortality rates from stroke than other ethnic groups. However, little is known about the prevalence of stroke risk factors in UK ethnic minority groups. We investigated the prevalence of these risk factors amongst African Caribbeans, black Africans and whites. Design: A random sample of patients aged 45-74 registered with 16 general practices in south London was surveyed in 1995. Main outcome measures were: prevalence of hypertension, mean serum cholesterol, serum fibrinogen and glycosylated haemoglobin AIC. Logistic and linear regressions were used to determine ethnic differences in these measures. Results: Hypertension was more prevalent in black Caribbeans (79.4%) and black Africans (71.6%) than in whites (54.3%) (p < 0.0001). There were ethnic group differences in mean random total cholesterol (p < 0.0001), triglycerides (p < 0.0001), fibrinogen (p = 0.03), HDL (p = 0.02) and HbAIC (p < 0.0001). Whites had higher mean random total cholesterol, triglycerides and fibrinogen than black Caribbeans but lower HDL and HbA1C. Black Africans had similar rates to black Caribbeans for these risk factors apart from lower triglvceride levels. Conclusion: These differences in risk factors may partially explain the high stroke mortality rates in black Caribbeans and black Africans compared to whites. There was little difference in prevalence of these risk factors between black Caribbean and black African groups. Specific strategies targeted to each ethnic group need to be developed to reduce risk factors. Design: Cross-sectional. Outcome measures: Age-standardised and sex-specific death rates and rate ratios 1979–83, 1989–93 and 1999–2003. Results: Coronary mortality fell among migrants, more so in the second decade than the first. Rate ratios for coronary mortality remained higher for men and women from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland and South Asia, and lower for men from Jamaica, other Caribbean countries, West Africa, Italy and Spain. Published in final edited form as: J Racial Ethn Health Disparities. 2018 Dec 13;6(3):487–496. doi: 10.1007/s40615-018-00547-8 Abstract Cardiovascular disease (CVD) disproportionately affects non-Hispanic blacks (NHB) in the United States (U.S.). Afro-Caribbean (AC) immigrants comprise over 50% of the immigrant black population and are critical in understanding the health trajectories of blacks in the U.S. We assessed the relationship between length of residence (proxy measure for acculturation) and cardiovascular health (CVH) based on the American Heart Association’s (AHA) seven ideal cardiovascular health components among AC immigrants in New York City (NYC). CVH scores were categorized into poor/intermediate CVH (0–3 components) or ideal CVH (≥ 4 components). Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the association between length of residence in the U.S. and poor/intermediate CVH. In adjusted models, the odds of poor/intermediate CVH were significantly higher for Guyanese (OR = 3.51; 95% CI 1.03–11.95) and Haitian immigrants (OR = 8.02; 95% CI 1.88–34.12) residing in the U.S. for ≥ 10 years than for those living in the U.S. for < 10 years. Length of residence was not significantly associated with CVH among Jamaican immigrants. We found evidence of ethnic differences in the association between acculturation and CVH among AC immigrants in a major metropolitan city. Culturally tailored interventions are needed to improve the CVH of AC immigrants as they become integrated into the U.S., with special consideration of country of birth. Keywords: Cardiovascular health, Afro-Caribbean, Immigrants, Acculturation Introduction Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading causes of death in the U.S. [1]. The American Heart Association (AHA) proposed the concept of “cardiovascular health” (CVH) to account for an individual’s total CVD risk profile using seven health metrics [1] including fasting plasma glucose, total cholesterol, blood pressure, body mass index (BMI), physical activity, diet, and smoking status [1]. Further, the AHA placed special emphasis on the significance of addressing disparities among underserved minority groups to expand its preventative goals [1]. Blacks in the U.S. have a significantly higher prevalence of CVD and known risk factors than any other racial/ethnic minority group [2]. By 2035, it is projected that blacks will have the highest rates of CVD in relation to other races [3]. Additionally, poor CVH is more common inBlacks in the U.S. [4, 5]. Blacks in the U.S. are a heterogeneous group comprised of African Americans, African, and Afro-Caribbean (AC) immigrants [6]. AC immigrants are those who trace their ancestry to both Africa and the Caribbean (West Indies) but are not Hispanic [7]. There are approximately four million AC immigrants in the U.S. who make up more than half of the immigrant black population [8, 9]. Although AC immigrants share similarities such as historical legacies of slavery and European colonialism [7], they differ in language, immigrant selectivity, migration patterns, economic and sociocultural backgrounds which influence health outcomes [10–13]. Jamaica has the largest number of black immigrants in the U.S. from the English-speaking Caribbean [9]. Jamaican immigration to the U.S. significantly increased in the late twentieth century and primarily included individuals with family ties in the U.S. and those seeking work visas; however, the most recent waves of immigrants from Jamaica include those in skilled and professional classes [8, 14]. Similar to Jamaican immigrants, Guyanese immigrants have migrated to the U.S. to avoid economic hardship in their native country; and have typically been comprised of a mixture of skilled, professional class, and domestic workers [15]. The theory asserts that assimilation is largely dependent on immigrant socioeconomic characteristics and the social context of the host country [22]. Evidence suggests that ethnicity, birthplace, sex, and age are all relevant to cardiovascular mortality differences, but the evidence base is mixed and often confounded by social and structural factors.

Ethnicity and birthplace contribute independently and interactively to cardiovascular mortality. In the UK and Wales evidence, coronary heart disease mortality was higher for migrants from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia, and lower for men from Jamaica, other Caribbean countries, West Africa, Italy, and Spain [N1-F2]. Stroke mortality remained higher for migrants overall, with some groups showing increasing disparities over time [N1-F2]. In the broader cardiovascular literature, South Asian but not black African or Caribbean individuals had higher CVD risk than white Europeans in UK Biobank, whereas in the same source, stroke mortality was reported as higher in black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites [N1-R3][N1-R4]. Taken together, this indicates that ethnicity is not a uniform risk factor: birthplace and country-of-origin effects can override or modify the observed pattern [N1-F2][N1-R3]. The evidence also suggests that Caribbean migrant groups, including Afro-Caribbean populations, may have complex patterns of risk, with some subgroups showing lower coronary mortality than native-born populations but persistent stroke burden [N1-F2].

Sex and age are important modifiers of mortality risk. In UK evidence, coronary mortality declined more slowly among Black Americans than White Americans, leading to higher rates for Black American women since the mid-1980s and Black American men since 2000 [N1-F2]. In the age-standardized evidence from England and Wales, coronary mortality fell among migrants, but the relative risk varied by sex and age group, with higher risk remaining for men and women from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia [N1-F2]. The age-standardized risk of death from CVD was also notably higher for men than women: 442/100,000 for men versus 246/100,000 for women [N2-R4]. These findings imply that sex and age should not be treated as mere ancillary variables; they often alter the magnitude and direction of ethnic differences [N2-R4][N1-F2].

Key confounders and adjustment strategies used in the evidence are well documented. The UK Biobank study explicitly adjusted for socioeconomic status (SES) and other confounders in describing all-cause and cardiovascular mortality by race and ethnicity [N2-R3]. The Heart article on migrant mortality in England and Wales relied on decennial census data and death records by country of birth, with analyses restricted to those aged 30–69 years due to small numbers at younger ages and poor denominator quality at older ages [N1-F2]. It also notes that traditional risk factors such as smoking or cholesterol levels only partially account for differences in cardiovascular risk, implying that adjustment for these is insufficient without broader social determinants [N1-F2]. The systematic review on ethnicity and place of birth also indicates that disparities can vary by country of origin and migration context, which matters because adjustment must include birthplace and country-specific social conditions [N2-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports regression, propensity score methods, and matching as common adjustment strategies, with the caution that race/ethnicity should not be interpreted casually in regressions controlling for confounding and mediating variables [N4-R4].

A major limitation is that ethnicity and birthplace are often treated as proxies for complex social exposures rather than biological markers. The Afro-Caribbean migrant literature emphasizes that migration history, socioeconomic background, and country of birth shape cardiovascular risk, and that these factors may interact with acculturation and social disadvantage [N3-R1][N3-F3]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. highlights that ethnic differences in acculturation and cardiovascular health are not uniform across subgroups, and that sociocultural differences, migration patterns, and economic background influence health outcomes [N3-F4]. This implies that ethnic categories may capture only part of the causal chain, and that birthplace and migration history are often necessary for accurate interpretation [N3-F4].

In short, the evidence supports a multivariate explanation: ethnicity and birthplace are major predictors, sex and age are modifiers, and confounders such as SES, traditional risk factors, and migration history are central to adjustment. However, the evidence is not yet sufficient to separate biological from structural pathways with certainty [N2-R3][N4-R4].

The observed mortality differences are notable, but they are not uniform across coronary heart disease, stroke, and all-cause cardiovascular mortality.

For Afro-Caribbean populations versus other ethnic groups, the evidence points to higher stroke mortality among people of African Caribbean descent compared to other ethnic groups [N1-F1]. The UK study found that black Caribbeans and black Africans had higher prevalence of hypertension, higher total cholesterol, lower HDL, and lower HbA1C than whites, and concluded that these risk factor differences may partially explain the higher stroke mortality rates in black Caribbeans and black Africans compared to whites [N1-F1]. In contrast, the UK Biobank evidence showed that South Asian, but not black African or Caribbean individuals, had higher CVD risk than white Europeans, while the same source also reported higher stroke mortality for black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites [N1-R3][N1-R4]. This suggests that Afro-Caribbean populations are often associated with higher stroke mortality relative to some other ethnic groups, but the evidence for coronary heart disease is more mixed.

For coronary heart disease, the evidence is more heterogeneous. In the England and Wales migrant mortality study, coronary mortality fell among migrants overall, but some groups remained higher relative to people born in England and Wales [N1-F2]. Specifically, men and women from Jamaica, other Caribbean countries, West Africa, Italy, and Spain had lower coronary mortality rate ratios than England/Wales-born people [N1-F2]. In contrast, men from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia had higher coronary mortality rate ratios [N1-F2]. The evidence also indicates that coronary mortality declined more slowly among Black Americans than White Americans, leading to higher rates for Black American women since the mid-1980s and for Black American men since 2000 [N1-F2]. This implies that Afro-Caribbean and related Black populations may have higher coronary mortality in some contexts, but not in others, and that the pattern depends on country, time period, and comparison group.

For stroke, the evidence is more consistently elevated in some migrant and Black populations. In England and Wales, stroke mortality remained higher for migrants, with increasing disparities for some groups over time [N1-F2]. The UK Biobank evidence also notes that stroke mortality was higher in black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites [N1-R4]. The broader mortality literature further reports that circulatory disease mortality was high among people born in Ireland, Scotland, Eastern Europe, East and West Africa, Bangladesh, India, or other regions [N5-R5]. In Scotland specifically, CHD mortality was substantially higher among people living in Scotland and born in Scotland, Ireland (North or South), India, or Pakistan [N5-R4]. This indicates that stroke mortality differences are not confined to Afro-Caribbean populations alone; they are part of a broader ethnic and birthplace-specific pattern.

The evidence also shows that mortality varies by age, sex, and geographic region or country. Age-standardized mortality was higher for men than women in the age-standardized CVD death rate study: 80% higher for men than for women [N2-R4]. In England and Wales, coronary mortality fell more slowly among Black Americans than White Americans, producing higher rates for Black American women since the mid-1980s and for Black American men since 2000 [N1-F2]. In the migrant mortality study, coronary mortality declined overall but the relative risk varied by sex and age group, with higher risk remaining for men and women from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia [N1-F2]. Regionally, the evidence indicates that coronary mortality was highest among migrants of Indian subcontinent origin in England and Wales, while stroke mortality was highest among Caribbean and directly African migrants [N1-F2]. Scotland had especially high CHD mortality among people born in Scotland and Ireland [N5-R4]. These findings show that mortality differences are not static: they are shaped by age, sex, and the specific geographic or national setting [N2-R4][N1-F2][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a consistent pattern that Afro-Caribbean and related Black populations often face higher stroke mortality relative to other ethnic groups, while coronary heart disease mortality varies more across groups and settings. All-cause cardiovascular mortality is also elevated for some migrant and ethnic groups, but the pattern is less uniform than for stroke [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R3][N5-R5].

The evidence base has important limitations, heterogeneity, and generalizability concerns.

Study design and population limitations are substantial. The migrant mortality study in England and Wales relied on decennial census data and death records by country of birth, with analyses restricted to those aged 30–69 years due to small numbers at younger ages and poor denominator quality at older ages [N1-F2]. This means the findings may not fully capture younger or older adults and may underrepresent groups with fewer deaths. The UK Biobank study used observational data and adjusted for socioeconomic status (SES) and other confounders, but it still depends on self-reported or administrative records and may not capture all causal pathways [N2-R3]. The systematic review on ethnicity and place of birth also relies on heterogeneous sources and can only report aggregate patterns rather than individual-level causal effects [N2-R2]. These design limitations reduce confidence in causal inference and highlight the importance of replication across settings.

Findings vary by country, setting, and measurement of ethnicity/birthplace. In England and Wales, coronary mortality declined among migrants, but the relative risk varied by group, with higher risk for Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia and lower risk for Jamaica, West Africa, Italy, and Spain [N1-F2]. In Scotland, CHD mortality was substantially higher among people born in Scotland and Ireland [N5-R4]. The broader mortality literature reports that circulatory disease mortality differed by country of birth in all age groups, including those aged ≥70 years [N5-R2]. The Afro-Caribbean literature shows that cardiovascular health outcomes differ by country of origin and by length of residence in the U.S., with evidence of ethnic differences in the association between acculturation and cardiovascular health [N3-F3]. These variations indicate that ethnicity and birthplace are not universal predictors; their effect depends on the population and setting [N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N3-F3].

Measurement of ethnicity and birthplace also affects conclusions. The migrant mortality evidence used country of birth and census-derived categories, which can be crude and may obscure subnational or subgroup differences [N1-F2]. The UK Biobank evidence used race and ethnicity as exposures, but the same source notes that race and ethnicity should not be interpreted casually in regressions controlling for confounding and mediating variables [N2-R3][N4-R4]. The Afro-Caribbean literature emphasizes that migration history, socioeconomic background, and country of birth shape cardiovascular risk, and that these factors may interact with acculturation and social disadvantage [N3-F3]. This means that the observed differences may reflect social and structural exposure gradients rather than purely biological differences [N3-F3].

What remains uncertain and why conclusions should be interpreted cautiously is clear. First, the evidence is not consistent across all populations and outcomes. Stroke mortality appears more consistently elevated in some Afro-Caribbean and Black populations, but coronary heart disease mortality varies more widely [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R3]. Second, traditional risk factors such as smoking or cholesterol levels only partially account for differences in cardiovascular risk, implying that adjustment for these is insufficient [N1-F2]. Third, the evidence is often observational and subject to residual confounding, especially because ethnicity is often used as an exposure variable in regressions that also control for confounders and mediating variables [N4-R4]. Fourth, the measurement of ethnicity and birthplace is often imprecise or context-dependent, which may lead to heterogeneous comparisons [N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4]. Overall, the evidence is useful but not definitive; conclusions should be interpreted cautiously because the findings depend on setting, measurement, and adjustment strategy [N2-R3][N4-R4][N5-R2].

The evidence points to multiple pathways linking ethnicity, birthplace, and cardiovascular risk, including biological, socioeconomic, and psychosocial mechanisms, as well as migration history, acculturation, and social disadvantage.

Biological pathways are evident but incomplete. The Afro-Caribbean literature notes that cardiovascular disease disproportionately affects non-Hispanic blacks in the U.S. and that Afro-Caribbean immigrants are a critical subgroup for understanding the health trajectories of blacks in the U.S. [N3-F3]. It also emphasizes that the etiology is primarily shaped by social determinants of health rather than genetics alone [N3-F4]. The UK Biobank evidence likewise reports higher CVD risk in South Asians and higher stroke mortality in black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites, suggesting that biological risk profiles may differ by ethnicity [N1-R3][N1-R4]. However, the evidence also indicates that traditional risk factors such as smoking or cholesterol levels only partially account for differences in cardiovascular risk, so biology alone cannot explain the full burden [N1-F2]. This implies that biological pathways are important, but they are often mediated by social and structural conditions.

Socioeconomic pathways are central. The Afro-Caribbean literature highlights that migration history, socioeconomic constraints, and acculturative stress meaningfully shape cardiovascular risk over time [N3-F3]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. notes that Afro-Caribbean immigrants comprise more than half of the Black immigrant population and that they differ in language, immigrant selectivity, migration patterns, and economic and sociocultural backgrounds, which influence health outcomes [N3-F3][N3-F4]. The migrant mortality evidence in England and Wales also points to poorer access to specialized clinical cardiovascular care and economic disadvantage contributing to trends in coronary mortality [N1-F2]. These findings support a socioeconomic pathway in which lower income, poorer access to care, and unfavorable working conditions increase cardiovascular risk [N3-F3][N1-F2].

Psychosocial pathways are also important. The Afro-Caribbean literature emphasizes that pre-migration exposure to racism and discrimination may negatively affect post-migration health [N3-R1]. Another source states that intersectionality emphasizes the significance of multiple stratifying systems, including racism and sexism, in shaping health outcomes [N3-R2]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. notes that broader societal issues such as racism and discrimination may influence negative health outcomes [N3-R5]. These sources collectively suggest that psychosocial stress, discrimination, and structural inequality are important mediators of cardiovascular risk among Afro-Caribbean populations [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

Migration history, acculturation, and social disadvantage are recurring themes. The Afro-Caribbean literature explicitly links length of residence (as a proxy for acculturation) to cardiovascular health, showing evidence of ethnic differences in the association between acculturation and cardiovascular health among Afro-Caribbean immigrants in New York City [N3-F3]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. also highlights segmented assimilation theory, noting that immigrants may assimilate into a middle class, an underclass, or selective assimilation, and that these pathways are shaped by immigrant socioeconomic characteristics and the host country context [N3-F4]. This indicates that migration history and acculturation are not neutral; they can either protect or increase cardiovascular risk depending on the social context [N3-F3][N3-F4].

Racism and discrimination are directly linked to cardiovascular health. The Afro-Caribbean literature notes that pre-migration exposure to racism and discrimination may negatively affect post-migration health [N3-R1]. It also states that broader societal issues such as racism and discrimination may influence negative health outcomes [N3-R5]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. similarly emphasizes that racism, socioeconomic constraints, and acculturative stress meaningfully shape cardiovascular risk over time [N3-F3]. These findings suggest that racism and discrimination operate as psychosocial stressors that may elevate cardiovascular risk through mechanisms such as chronic stress, poor coping, and reduced access to resources [N3-R1][N3-R5][N3-F3].

In conclusion, the evidence supports a multifactorial model: ethnicity and birthplace are markers of broader social disadvantage and migration history, which interact with socioeconomic, psychosocial, and biological pathways to influence cardiovascular risk. Racism and discrimination appear especially important as mediators, while acculturation, migration patterns, and social disadvantage shape the overall risk profile [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F3][N3-F4].

## Integrated synthesis of mortality differences, contributing factors, and the overall evidence base

The evidence suggests that Afro-Caribbean populations, and related Black populations in the UK and U.S., often face different patterns of coronary heart disease (CHD) and stroke mortality relative to other ethnic groups. The overall picture is not uniform: stroke mortality is consistently elevated in some Afro-Caribbean and Black populations, while coronary heart disease mortality varies more across groups and settings [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R3][N1-R4]. All-cause cardiovascular mortality is also elevated for some migrant and ethnic groups, but the pattern is less consistent than for stroke [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R3][N5-R5]. At the same time, the evidence is mixed, heterogeneous, and often limited by design, measurement, and confounding issues [N2-R3][N2-R2][N4-R4][N5-R2][N5-R4].

---

## 1) What the observed mortality differences are

### Stroke mortality
The evidence points to higher stroke mortality among people of African Caribbean descent compared to other ethnic groups. In London, black Caribbeans and black Africans had higher prevalence of hypertension, higher total cholesterol, lower HDL, and lower HbA1C than whites, and these risk factor differences were interpreted as partially explaining the higher stroke mortality rates in black Caribbeans and black Africans compared to whites [N1-F1]. In broader UK Biobank evidence, South Asian, but not black African or Caribbean individuals, had higher CVD risk than white Europeans, while stroke mortality was higher in black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites [N1-R3][N1-R4]. This suggests that Afro-Caribbean populations are often associated with higher stroke mortality relative to some other ethnic groups [N1-F1][N1-R4].

### Coronary heart disease mortality
For coronary heart disease, the evidence is more heterogeneous. In England and Wales, coronary mortality fell among migrants overall, but some groups remained higher relative to people born in England and Wales [N1-F2]. Specifically, men and women from Jamaica, other Caribbean countries, West Africa, Italy, and Spain had lower coronary mortality rate ratios than England/Wales-born people, while men from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia had higher coronary mortality rate ratios [N1-F2]. In the same source, coronary mortality declined more slowly among Black Americans than White Americans, leading to higher rates for Black American women since the mid-1980s and for Black American men since 2000 [N1-F2]. This indicates that Afro-Caribbean and related Black populations may have higher coronary mortality in some contexts, but not in others, and that the pattern depends on country, time period, and comparison group [N1-F2].

### All-cause cardiovascular mortality
The evidence also shows that all-cause cardiovascular mortality is elevated for some migrant and ethnic groups. In England and Wales, stroke mortality remained higher for migrants, with increasing disparities for some groups over time [N1-F2]. In Scotland, CHD mortality was substantially higher among people living in Scotland and born in Scotland, Ireland (North or South), India, or Pakistan [N5-R4]. More broadly, circulatory disease mortality was high among people born in Ireland, Scotland, Eastern Europe, East and West Africa, Bangladesh, India, or other regions [N5-R5]. This indicates that cardiovascular mortality differences are not confined to Afro-Caribbean populations alone; they are part of a broader ethnic and birthplace-specific pattern [N1-F2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

### Variation by age, sex, and geography
Mortality differences are also shaped by age, sex, and geography. Age-standardized CVD mortality was notably higher for men than women: 80% higher for men than for women [N2-R4]. In England and Wales, coronary mortality declined more slowly among Black Americans than White Americans, producing higher rates for Black American women since the mid-1980s and for Black American men since 2000 [N1-F2]. In the migrant mortality study, coronary mortality declined overall but the relative risk varied by sex and age group, with higher risk remaining for men and women from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia [N1-F2]. Regionally, coronary mortality was highest among migrants of Indian subcontinent origin in England and Wales, while stroke mortality was highest among Caribbean and directly African migrants [N1-F2]. Scotland had especially high CHD mortality among people born in Scotland and Ireland [N5-R4]. These findings show that mortality differences are not static: they are shaped by age, sex, and the specific geographic or national setting [N2-R4][N1-F2][N5-R4].

---

## 2) Which factors explain differences in mortality across ethnic groups

### Ethnicity and birthplace: independent and interactive contributors
Ethnicity and birthplace are major contributors, but they often interact rather than act independently. In England and Wales, coronary mortality fell among migrants, but the relative risk varied by group, with higher risk for Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia and lower risk for Jamaica, other Caribbean countries, West Africa, Italy, and Spain [N1-F2]. In Scotland, CHD mortality was substantially higher among people living in Scotland and born in Scotland, Ireland, India, or Pakistan [N5-R4]. The UK Biobank evidence similarly found that South Asian, but not black African or Caribbean individuals, had higher CVD risk than white Europeans, while stroke mortality was higher in black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites [N1-R3][N1-R4]. Taken together, these findings indicate that ethnicity is not a uniform risk factor: birthplace and country-of-origin effects can override or modify the observed pattern [N1-F2][N1-R3].

### Sex and age: important modifiers
Sex and age are important modifiers of mortality risk. In the age-standardized evidence, coronary mortality was 80% higher for men than women [N2-R4]. In England and Wales, coronary mortality declined more slowly among Black Americans than White Americans, leading to higher rates for Black American women since the mid-1980s and for Black American men since 2000 [N1-F2]. In the migrant mortality study, coronary mortality declined overall but the relative risk varied by sex and age group, with higher risk remaining for men and women from Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia [N1-F2]. These findings imply that sex and age should not be treated as mere ancillary variables; they often alter the magnitude and direction of ethnic differences [N2-R4][N1-F2].

### Key confounders and adjustment strategies
The evidence also shows that adjustment is central to interpreting ethnic differences. The UK Biobank study explicitly adjusted for socioeconomic status (SES) and other confounders in describing all-cause and cardiovascular mortality by race and ethnicity [N2-R3]. The migrant mortality study in England and Wales relied on decennial census data and death records by country of birth, with analyses restricted to those aged 30–69 years due to small numbers at younger ages and poor denominator quality at older ages [N1-F2]. It also notes that traditional risk factors such as smoking or cholesterol levels only partially account for differences in cardiovascular risk, implying that adjustment for these is insufficient without broader social determinants [N1-F2]. The systematic review on ethnicity and place of birth indicates that disparities can vary by country of origin and migration context, which matters because adjustment must include birthplace and country-specific social conditions [N2-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports regression, propensity score methods, and matching as common adjustment strategies, with the caution that race/ethnicity should not be interpreted casually in regressions controlling for confounding and mediating variables [N4-R4].

### Bottom line on explanation
The evidence supports a multivariate explanation: ethnicity and birthplace are major predictors, sex and age are modifiers, and confounders such as SES, traditional risk factors, and migration history are central to adjustment. However, the evidence is not yet sufficient to separate biological from structural pathways with certainty [N2-R3][N4-R4].

---

## 3) Limitations, heterogeneity, and generalizability

### Study design and population limitations
The evidence base has substantial limitations. The migrant mortality study in England and Wales relied on decennial census data and death records by country of birth, with analyses restricted to those aged 30–69 years due to small numbers at younger ages and poor denominator quality at older ages [N1-F2]. This means the findings may not fully capture younger or older adults and may underrepresent groups with fewer deaths. The UK Biobank evidence used observational data and adjusted for SES and other confounders, but it still depends on self-reported or administrative records and may not capture all causal pathways [N2-R3]. The systematic review on ethnicity and place of birth also relies on heterogeneous sources and can only report aggregate patterns rather than individual-level causal effects [N2-R2]. These design limitations reduce confidence in causal inference and highlight the importance of replication across settings [N2-R3][N2-R2].

### Heterogeneity across countries, settings, and measurement
Findings vary by country, setting, and measurement of ethnicity/birthplace. In England and Wales, coronary mortality declined among migrants, but the relative risk varied by group, with higher risk for Scotland, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland, and South Asia and lower risk for Jamaica, other Caribbean countries, West Africa, Italy, and Spain [N1-F2]. In Scotland, CHD mortality was substantially higher among people born in Scotland and Ireland [N5-R4]. The broader mortality literature reports that circulatory disease mortality differed by country of birth in all age groups, including those aged ≥70 years [N5-R2]. The Afro-Caribbean literature shows that cardiovascular health outcomes differ by country of origin and by length of residence in the U.S., with evidence of ethnic differences in the association between acculturation and cardiovascular health [N3-F3]. These variations indicate that ethnicity and birthplace are not universal predictors; their effect depends on the population and setting [N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N3-F3].

### Measurement issues
Measurement of ethnicity and birthplace also affects conclusions. The migrant mortality evidence used country of birth and census-derived categories, which can be crude and may obscure subnational or subgroup differences [N1-F2]. The UK Biobank evidence used race and ethnicity as exposures, but the same source notes that race and ethnicity should not be interpreted casually in regressions controlling for confounding and mediating variables [N2-R3][N4-R4]. The Afro-Caribbean literature emphasizes that migration history, socioeconomic background, and country of birth shape cardiovascular risk, and that these factors may interact with acculturation and social disadvantage [N3-F3]. This means that the observed differences may reflect social and structural exposure gradients rather than purely biological differences [N3-F3].

### What remains uncertain
What remains uncertain is that the evidence is not consistent across all populations and outcomes. Stroke mortality appears more consistently elevated in some Afro-Caribbean and Black populations, but coronary heart disease mortality varies more widely [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R3]. Traditional risk factors such as smoking or cholesterol levels only partially account for differences in cardiovascular risk, implying that adjustment for these is insufficient [N1-F2]. The evidence is often observational and subject to residual confounding, especially because ethnicity is often used as an exposure variable in regressions that also control for confounders and mediating variables [N4-R4]. The measurement of ethnicity and birthplace is often imprecise or context-dependent, which may lead to heterogeneous comparisons [N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4]. Overall, the evidence is useful but not definitive; conclusions should be interpreted cautiously because the findings depend on setting, measurement, and adjustment strategy [N2-R3][N4-R4][N5-R2].

---

## 4) Pathways and mechanisms linking ethnicity, birthplace, and cardiovascular risk

### Biological, socioeconomic, and psychosocial pathways
The evidence points to multiple pathways linking ethnicity, birthplace, and cardiovascular risk, including biological, socioeconomic, and psychosocial mechanisms. The Afro-Caribbean literature notes that cardiovascular disease disproportionately affects non-Hispanic blacks in the U.S. and that Afro-Caribbean immigrants are a critical subgroup for understanding the health trajectories of blacks in the U.S. [N3-F3]. It also emphasizes that the etiology is primarily shaped by social determinants of health rather than genetics alone [N3-F4]. The UK Biobank evidence likewise reports higher CVD risk in South Asians and higher stroke mortality in black Caribbean and black African groups compared to whites, suggesting that biological risk profiles may differ by ethnicity [N1-R3][N1-R4]. However, the evidence also indicates that traditional risk factors such as smoking or cholesterol levels only partially account for differences in cardiovascular risk, so biology alone cannot explain the full burden [N1-F2]. This implies that biological pathways are important, but they are often mediated by social and structural conditions [N3-F3][N1-F2].

### Socioeconomic pathways
Socioeconomic pathways are central. The Afro-Caribbean literature highlights that migration history, socioeconomic constraints, and acculturative stress meaningfully shape cardiovascular risk over time [N3-F3]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. notes that Afro-Caribbean immigrants comprise more than half of the Black immigrant population and that they differ in language, immigrant selectivity, migration patterns, and economic and sociocultural backgrounds, which influence health outcomes [N3-F3][N3-F4]. The migrant mortality evidence in England and Wales also points to poorer access to specialized clinical cardiovascular care and economic disadvantage contributing to trends in coronary mortality [N1-F2]. These findings support a socioeconomic pathway in which lower income, poorer access to care, and unfavorable working conditions increase cardiovascular risk [N3-F3][N1-F2].

### Psychosocial pathways
Psychosocial pathways are also important. The Afro-Caribbean literature emphasizes that pre-migration exposure to racism and discrimination may negatively affect post-migration health [N3-R1]. Another source states that intersectionality emphasizes the significance of multiple stratifying systems, including racism and sexism, in shaping health outcomes [N3-R2]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. likewise notes that broader societal issues such as racism and discrimination may influence negative health outcomes [N3-R5]. These sources collectively suggest that psychosocial stress, discrimination, and structural inequality are important mediators of cardiovascular risk among Afro-Caribbean populations [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

### Migration history, acculturation, and social disadvantage
Migration history, acculturation, and social disadvantage are recurring themes. The Afro-Caribbean literature explicitly links length of residence (as a proxy for acculturation) to cardiovascular health, showing evidence of ethnic differences in the association between acculturation and cardiovascular health among Afro-Caribbean immigrants in New York City [N3-F3]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. also highlights segmented assimilation theory, noting that immigrants may assimilate into a middle class, an underclass, or selective assimilation, and that these pathways are shaped by immigrant socioeconomic characteristics and the host country context [N3-F4]. This indicates that migration history and acculturation are not neutral; they can either protect or increase cardiovascular risk depending on the social context [N3-F3][N3-F4].

### Racism and discrimination
Racism and discrimination are directly linked to cardiovascular health. The Afro-Caribbean literature notes that pre-migration exposure to racism and discrimination may negatively affect post-migration health [N3-R1]. It also states that broader societal issues such as racism and discrimination may influence negative health outcomes [N3-R5]. The systematic literature review on Afro-Caribbean immigrants in the U.S. similarly emphasizes that racism, socioeconomic constraints, and acculturative stress meaningfully shape cardiovascular risk over time [N3-F3]. These findings suggest that racism and discrimination operate as psychosocial stressors that may elevate cardiovascular risk through mechanisms such as chronic stress, poor coping, and reduced access to resources [N3-R1][N3-R5][N3-F3].

---

## 5) Overall conclusion

The overall evidence suggests that Afro-Caribbean populations often face higher stroke mortality relative to other ethnic groups, while coronary heart disease mortality varies more across groups and settings [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R3][N1-R4]. The differences are influenced by ethnicity, birthplace, sex, and age, with ethnicity and birthplace acting as major predictors, sex and age as modifiers, and socioeconomic, psychosocial, and biological pathways as important mechanisms [N2-R3][N2-R4][N3-F3][N3-F4]. The evidence is strongest for stroke and less consistent for coronary heart disease, with important regional and subgroup variation [N1-F2][N5-R4][N5-R5]. However, the evidence base is limited by study design, measurement, and confounding issues, and conclusions should be interpreted cautiously because findings vary by country, setting, and how ethnicity/birthplace are measured [N2-R2][N4-R4][N5-R2].

In short: Afro-Caribbean populations are not a single homogeneous group with uniform cardiovascular risk; they are shaped by country of origin, migration history, socioeconomic disadvantage, psychosocial stress, and structural inequality. The evidence supports a multicausal model in which ethnicity and birthplace are markers of broader social disadvantage, and cardiovascular risk arises from biological, socioeconomic, and psychosocial pathways operating together [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F3][N3-F4].
